To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
spatial skills training can enhance reading comprehension in lower SES children who are 3 to 5 years behind their same aged peers on standardized reading measures.

the spatially trained group outperformed both the reading only and control groups on all measures of reading comprehension and that the spatially skilled respondents outperformed the reading only group on measures of space relations and abstract rea soning.

spatial skills training, as a supplement to a reading comprehension remediation program, significantly enhanced gains in reading comprehension, and that these gains were not attributable to the effects of the spatial training per se.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a possible causal relationship between basic spatial skills and the subsequent development of higher order cognitive abilities.
the possibility that basic spatial abilities might provide an important but previously unexploited basis for improving reading skills and, ultimately, reading comprehension.
the possibility that basic spatial skills might be a necessary condition for the acquisition of higher order cognitive skills, such as reading comprehension.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is not yet in, and the question of whether spatial skills training can facilitate the development of reading comprehension skills remains open.
the present results support the hypothesis that spatial training can facilitate reading comprehension in a group of lower SES adolescents who are 3 to 5 years behind their same-aged peers.

the present findings suggest the potential for spatial skills training to enhance reading comprehension, but that the effects of such training are limited to the reading comprehension domain and that they are not generalizable to other cognitive domains.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
spatial skills training is an effective and cost-efficient means of improving reading performance, particularly in low SES children.

we found that the children who were given training in spatial skills, in addition to reading training, showed a significant improvement in reading comprehension, as compared with the children who received only reading training, and the children who received no training at all.
the spatially trained children made greater gains than the other two groups in the acquisition of the more advanced cognitive skills.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatial skills of the students were improved by the intervention and this improvement was associated with an increase in reading comprehension.
spatial training can help students who are struggling with reading, and that the training can be delivered in a way that is cost effective.
spatial training can help kids with reading comprehension.
